query: For an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in its uniform, fine lamellar state, whose strength and plasticity remain below industrial application requirements, what single intervention could improve performance for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive conditions? State the proposed intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the starting alloy, applicable operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: A low‐temperature aging heat treatment that induces the in situ precipitation of uniformly dispersed, nanoscale coherent L12 intermetallic phases in the eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy will enhance yield strength, creep resistance, and overall performance (while maintaining ductility) for fastener applications under harsh service conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Fine lamellar eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy produced by cold rolling and recrystallization, with a predominantly uniform lamellar structure and B2 precipitates largely confined to grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: Apply a carefully optimized low-temperature aging heat treatment (e.g., around 600–700°C for a controlled duration under an inert atmosphere) aimed at precipitating nanoscale coherent L12 intermetallic phases uniformly within the fcc lamellae.
generation.conditions: The treatment should be applied after obtaining a recrystallized, fine-lamellar microstructure. Subsequent performance should be evaluated under conditions simulating extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive environments typical of fastener applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale, coherent L12 precipitates distributed within the fcc lamella.
generation.mechanism: The coherent L12 precipitates act as strong obstacles to dislocation motion via mechanisms such as Orowan bowing, thereby increasing the yield strength and retarding room-temperature creep. This added precipitation strengthening, complementary to the existing grain boundary strengthening, can help maintain or slightly improve ductility while enhancing overall mechanical stability under cyclic, corrosive, and high-load conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the starting alloy, the aged alloy is expected to exhibit a significant increase in yield strength and improved creep resistance, while preserving an acceptable level of ductility, making it more suitable for fasteners exposed to harsh operational environments.
generation.baseline: The as-processed fine lamellar eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, which exhibits strength and plasticity levels below industrial application requirements.
generation.boundary: The predicted improvements apply when the aging treatment parameters are optimized to promote nanoscale L12 precipitation without causing grain coarsening or excessive precipitate growth that could embrittle the alloy; improvements must be validated under simulated service conditions (extreme temperature cycling, long-term loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive exposure).
generation.uncertainty: While evidence supports the potential benefits of precipitation strengthening by nanoscale L12 phases, previous reports indicate that in similar alloys the contribution of precipitation to overall strength has been modest compared to grain boundary strengthening. Thus, the magnitude of improvement and its balance with ductility must be carefully optimized, and the exact aging parameters may require further refinement.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several batches of the fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy. Subject one set to the optimized low-temperature aging treatment (with systematic variations in temperature and time to refine the precipitation process) and keep a control set untreated. Then, simulate service conditions by subjecting both sets to cyclic temperature extreme variations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep tests, and corrosive environment exposures.
measurements: Mechanical testing: quasi-static tensile tests to measure yield strength, ductility, and work hardening; creep tests at room temperature; and dynamic loading tests.
Microstructure analysis by TEM and XRD to confirm the formation, size, and distribution of nanoscale L12 precipitates.
Corrosion resistance assessments under simulated corrosive conditions.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged specimens do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in yield strength and creep resistance compared to the untreated control, or if the aging treatment results in undesirable grain coarsening or precipitate morphology that compromises ductility and corrosion resistance, the hypothesis is considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Recent studies indicate that eutectic high-entropy alloys can simultaneously possess high strength and high ductility, which have potential industrial applications. The present study focuses on Al0.7CoCrFeNi, a lamellar dual-phase (fcc + B2) precipitation-strengthenable eutectic high entropy alloy. This alloy exhibits an fcc + B2 (B2 with bcc nano-precipitates) microstructure resulting in a combination of the soft and ductile fcc phase together with hard B2 phase. Low temperature annealing leads to the precipitation of ordered L12 intermetallic precipitates within the fcc resulting in enhanced strength. The strengthening contribution due to fine scale L12 is modeled using Orowan dislocation bowing and by-pass mechanism. The alloy was tested under quasi-static (strain-rate = 10−3 s−1) tensile loading and dynamic (strain-rate = 103 s−1) compressive loading. Due to the fine lamellar microstructure with a large number of fcc-bcc interfaces, the alloy show relatively high flow-stresses, ~1400 MPa under quasi-static loading and in excess of 1800 MPa under dynamic loading. The current work is the first investigation of shear deformation in a eutectic HEAs (EHEAs) and effect of precipitation strengthening on the formation of ASBs in any alloy. The fcc phase in the lamellar two-phase microstructure is strengthened by formation of ordered L12 nano-precipitates by an additional low temperature aging, without compromising the tensile ductility of the alloy. We used gun pressures ranging from 10 psi to 40 psi to shoot the Kolsky bar in the SHPB apparatus resulting in increasing displacement rate (velocity of deformation). The width of the ASB increased as the gun pressure was increased. The precipitation of L12 phase did not delay the formation of ASB or affect the ASB width, however, the deformed region around ASB, consisting of high density of twinning in fcc phase, was reduced from 80 µm to 20 µm in the stronger precipitation strengthened condition. Nano-indentation results showed the change in hardness of the fcc and B2 phases before and after deformation and variation of hardness across the ASB.

In this study, the microstructures and mechanical properties of Al0.3CoCrFeNi HEAs after cold rolling and subsequent annealing at 800, 900, and 1000 °C were systematically investigated. The detailed conclusions were draw as follows. (1) The microstructures in 800 °C-, 900 °C-, and 1000 °C-annealed specimens showed the partial recrystallization, full recrystallization, and grain coarsening, respectively. (2) Two types of B2 phases were precipitated after cold rolling and subsequent annealing. The sizes of B2 precipitates along the grain boundaries increased but their volume fractions decreased with increasing the annealing temperature. These grain-boundary precipitates refined the grain sizes into the quasi ultra-fine grain regime (~0.9 μm) and fine grain regime (~2.2 and ~7.2 μm) in 800 °C-, 900 °C-, and 1000 °C-annealed specimens. (3) The 900 °C- and 1000 °C-annealed specimens with the recrystallized grains and B2 precipitates possessed the higher strength than the as-cast one. The precipitation strengthening contributions were calculated to occupy ~10.5% and ~9.1% of yield strengths, respectively.
